newsitem.title: USA: John Duffey of bluegrass group Seldom Scene dies.
newsitem.headline: John Duffey of bluegrass group Seldom Scene dies.

text.p: John Duffey, whose "high lonesome tenor" and sparkling mandolin playing helped propel the Seldom Scene bluegrass group to stardom, has died, a member of the group said on Wednesday. He was 62.
Duffey died on Tuesday in Arlington, Virginia, without regaining consciousness after suffering an apparent heart attack at his home, Dudley Connell, current lead singer with the group, said.

Connell described Duffey as "one of the half-dozen most important players ever in this industry. He helped redefine how people looked at bluegrass, made it acceptable to the urban masses by his choice of material and style of performance."

Duffey, a native of Washington, formed the Seldom Scene in 1971 after about a decade of playing with Charlie Waller and the Country Gentlemen, another Washington-based bluegrass group that gained fame in the 1960s.

A music instrument repairman who always complained about the travel that seemed an inherent part of the music business, Duffey put together the Seldom Scene with four other Washington musicians who had demanding day jobs -- physician John Starling, mathematician Ben Eldridge, graphic artist Mike Auldridge, and National Geographic mapmaker Tom Gray.

The group planned to play occasionally, which was why they chose the name Seldom Scene. But a regular Thursday night gig with standing-room only crowds at a club in Bethesda, Maryland, led to demands for recording and road appearances, and then to weekly appearances at an Alexandria, Virginia, club, the Birchmere, where they played for 22 years.
Other members of the group said Duffey's quirky, commanding stage presence was the secret to their success.

Over a quarter-century the group played in most of the 50 states and many other countries, including Japan and France, and made dozens of recordings, the most recent of which was "Dream Scene" released this fall. They also played for presidents Jimmy Carter and Ronald Reagan.
Duffey's father sang at the Metropolitan Opera in New York and band members said he was never enthusiastic about his son's interest in what he called "hillbilly music."
Duffey, along with Waller and other original Country Gentlemen, was inducted into the International Bluegrass Music Associations's Hall of Fame in September.
